title: Effective theories: proof search and decision procedures

based_on.title: An Introduction to Gödel’s Theorems
based_on.pages: 33–35 (§§4.3–4.5, Theorems 4.1–4.2); 304–306 (§40.5, Theorems 40.6–40.7); corrected second-edition reprint, August 2020

summary: Enumerate formal consequences, turn completeness into a terminating proof search, and decide equality and dense-order sentences by explicit quantifier elimination.
abstract: Given a sentence and an axiom-enumerating program, when can a computation settle whether the sentence follows from those axioms? In a fixed finite language with effective syntax coding, computably enumerable axioms make theoremhood recognizable by proof search: every proof will eventually be found, although the search may continue forever when no proof exists. If the axioms are consistent and prove each sentence or its negation, searching for both proofs together gives a decision procedure. Consistency rules out contradictory answers, and the ability to prove one side ensures termination. More direct algorithms decide sentences about infinite sets with equality alone and about nonempty dense linear orders without endpoints. They eliminate quantifiers by finite operations on formulas, reducing sentence truth to a Boolean calculation. These examples identify the additional information that turns a general recognition procedure into a terminating decision.
